596.title: the cave of Svayamprabha
596.hook: lost, thirsty, and following wet birds into the dark
596.howItsDone: Svayamprabha is remembered as one of the Ramayana's ascetic women, alongside Shabari; in many retellings her cave is a short, mysterious interlude before the search reaches the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's ring went south with Hanuman, three parties came home empty, and everyone waits on the south.

The southern party is having a terrible time. They've searched the Vindhya hills, forest after forest, cave after cave. Nothing. Now they're lost, hungry and desperately thirsty, in dry country with no stream in sight, and the month is running out. Then they see birds flying out of a hole in the hillside: cranes, geese, waterbirds, their wings wet. Where there are wet birds, there's water somewhere. So in they go.
screen: `LOST IN THE VINDHYA HILLS.` → `THIRSTY.` → `WET BIRDS FROM A HOLE.`

segments.voice: The cave is dark and overgrown with creepers. Valmiki calls it Rikshabila, the bear's hole. Hanuman goes first. The monkeys hold on to one another in the pitch black and go deeper and deeper, with no idea what's at the end. And then light. They come out into a place that shouldn't exist underground: golden trees glowing like fire, palaces of gold and silver, lotus pools, and heaps of food, fruit and honey. In the middle of it all sits a woman ascetic, dressed in bark and black antelope skin, shining with her own light. Hanuman approaches with joined palms and asks: whose place is this? She tells them. It was built by Maya, the great architect of the demons, by his own powers. He lived here with Hema, a celestial dancer, until Indra killed him. Now it belongs to Hema. And I, she says, am Svayamprabha, daughter of Merusavarni. I keep it for my friend. Her name means shining by herself. Then comes what she does next. She doesn't question them or test them. Eat first, she says. Drink. Rest. Then tell me your story. Lost travelers, fed by an ascetic in a hidden golden city, and nothing asked of them first.
screen: `INTO THE BEAR'S HOLE.` · `HOLDING ON IN THE DARK.` · `A GOLDEN CITY BUILT BY MAYA.` · `EAT FIRST, THEN TALK.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip; if not, just notice your mouth and throat. Breathe in and remember the parched monkeys following wet wings into the dark; breathe out and let the sip, or the breath, be enough. Then sit like a guest who was given what they needed before anyone asked a single question.
Svayamprabha, 'self-shining': the ascetic who keeps a golden city hidden in a cave, and feeds the lost monkeys before asking who they are.
Your line: eat first, then talk. For lost travelers, kindness came before any questions. Until tomorrow.

597.title: the cave of Svayamprabha
597.hook: cover your eyes, and you're out, but the month is gone
597.carry: some help asks you to stop looking
597.howItsDone: Some later tellings, such as the Adhyatma Ramayana, have Svayamprabha go on to meet Rama; in Valmiki she simply goes back into her cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a golden city underground, and Svayamprabha's welcome: eat first, then talk.

Fed and rested, the monkeys tell Svayamprabha everything: Rama, Sita, Ravana, the search, Sugriva's deadline. She listens. And then Hanuman asks the question that's been sitting under all that good food. How do we get out? They came in by holding each other in the dark, through a long, twisting passage. It's not easy to leave this place alive, Svayamprabha tells them. Not without help. Then she says she'll help.
screen: `THEY TELL HER EVERYTHING.` → `HOW DO WE GET OUT?` → `NOT WITHOUT HELP.`

segments.voice: Svayamprabha says she'll bring them out by the power of her austerities. Close your eyes, she says. Cover them with your hands. They do. And in an instant they're outside, standing near the shore, with the great southern ocean roaring in front of them. She shows them where they are, wishes them well, and goes back into her cave. Some help asks you to stop looking. The monkeys couldn't watch the way out; they could only let themselves be taken. Then the cruel part. Inside the cave it didn't feel long. But outside the trees are in flower, and when Angada counts the days, the month Sugriva gave them is gone. They've been away too long, and they still have nothing to report. And look at what Svayamprabha asks in return. Nothing. In a book full of bargains, a pact for a pact, a ring for trust, an army for a kingdom, she gives food, rest and rescue, and walks back into the dark. Valmiki tells us very little more about her. She appears for a few chapters, helps, and is gone. The epic has other helpers like that: an old vulture who fights and falls, a woman waiting in a forest hermitage, an ascetic in a cave. And now, on the shore, with the sea in front of them and the deadline behind them, the southern party has a new problem.
screen: `CLOSE YOUR EYES.` · `OUT BY THE SOUTHERN SEA.` · `THE MONTH IS GONE.` · `SHE ASKS NOTHING IN RETURN.`

segments.voice: Cover your eyes gently with your palms, if that's comfortable, or simply close them, and feel the warm dark. Breathe in and let yourself not look, not plan, not check; breathe out and trust the next moment to arrive on its own. When you're ready, lower your hands and keep sitting with soft eyes.
Svayamprabha, who leads the monkeys out of her cave by her own power. Eyes covered, and they're out by the southern sea, but the month is already gone.

598.title: the cave of Svayamprabha
598.hook: late, empty-handed, and tempted to hide or give up
598.carry: a line of monkeys on the shore
598.howItsDone: Prayopavesha, fasting unto death, appears in the epics as a solemn vow; Hindu teachers today speak of it only in very specific traditional contexts, and in the Ramayana the monkeys' vow is interrupted before it's carried out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Svayamprabha led them out with eyes covered and asked nothing back. But the month was already gone.

On the beach, Angada does the math, and it's bad. They're late. They haven't found Sita. Sugriva warned that anyone who came back late would answer with their life. And Angada carries a private fear on top of that. He's Vali's son. His uncle took his father's throne with Rama's help. Angada wonders whether Sugriva has ever really trusted him. Back late and empty-handed? He decides he isn't going back at all.
screen: `ANGADA DOES THE MATH.` → `A PRIVATE FEAR.` → `HE WON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Despair spreads fast. Angada tells the others he'll fast to death right here on the shore, a vow called prayopavesha, sitting down to die without food. One of the monkeys, named Tara, a different Tara from Vali's widow, offers another way out: let's go back to the cave. It has everything, food, water, safety. We could live there forever and no one could reach us. Several monkeys like the idea. Then Hanuman speaks. He sees the group about to split. To Angada he's gentle: Sugriva is fair, and you're dear to him; don't assume the worst. About the cave he's blunt: Lakshmana's arrows could split that cave open. Hiding isn't safety. And Valmiki says Hanuman quietly wins the others over, one by one, so they won't follow Angada into the cave. It doesn't fully work. Angada isn't convinced. He spreads sacred darbha grass on the shore and sits down to die, and the other monkeys sit down with him, a long line of them along the sea, waiting. They start to talk about how they got here. About Rama. About Sita. About Kaikeyi's demand, and Dasharatha's death. And about Jatayu, the old vulture who died fighting Ravana. And up on the hillside behind them, out of a cave, something very old is listening.
screen: `PRAYOPAVESHA: A FAST TO DEATH.` · `THE PULL BACK TO THE CAVE.` · `HANUMAN: HIDING ISN'T SAFETY.` · `A LINE OF MONKEYS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Notice, gently, whether there's somewhere in your life you've quietly given up, not to fix it now, just to see it. Breathe in and name it; breathe out and let one person's voice come to mind who would tell you, kindly, not to quit yet. If giving up ever feels like more than that, please reach out today: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

Your line: a line of monkeys on the shore. Even here, the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.

599.title: Sampati
599.hook: a hungry old vulture hears his brother's name
599.howItsDone: Sampati and Jatayu are often told about together in Ramayana storytelling, as two brothers who both serve Rama: one by fighting Ravana, one by seeing where he went.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Svayamprabha's cave behind them, a line of monkeys sat down on the shore to fast, talking about Jatayu.
screen: `A LINE OF MONKEYS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Out of a cave on the hillside comes an enormous old bird. What's left of his wings is burned. He drags himself onto the rocks and looks down at a beach covered with monkeys, all sitting perfectly still. And he says to himself, more or less: what luck. A meal, lined up and waiting to die. As each one goes, I'll eat him. The monkeys hear him. Nobody on that beach is sitting quite so still anymore.
screen: `AN OLD BIRD ON THE ROCKS.` → `BURNED WINGS.` → `WHAT LUCK: A MEAL.`

segments.voice: The monkeys are terrified. Angada, already in despair, says it aloud to Hanuman: death has come for us in the shape of a bird. Still lamenting, he names Jatayu again. Even Jatayu gave his life for Rama, he says. We're dying for Rama too. The old bird freezes. Who is speaking of my brother? he calls down. I haven't heard that name in so long. Is Jatayu dead? How did it happen? The hunter has become a mourner. His name is Sampati, and Jatayu was his younger brother. He asks them to help him down from the hill, and the monkeys, still uneasy, do. Angada tells him the whole story: Rama's exile, Sita taken, Jatayu's fight with Ravana in the sky, his death, and the funeral Rama gave him. Sampati grieves for his brother right there on the beach. Watch how the story travels. Jatayu's death looked like a defeat months ago in the story. Now it saves the whole southern party: because they spoke his name, the bird who meant to eat them asks to hear more. In this poem, nothing given for Rama seems to go to waste.
screen: `ANGADA NAMES JATAYU.` · `WHO SPEAKS OF MY BROTHER?` · `SAMPATI GRIEVES ON THE BEACH.` · `NOTHING GIVEN GOES TO WASTE.`

segments.voice: Think of a name that matters to you, someone you've lost touch with, or lost, and say it silently. Breathe in and notice what happens in your chest; breathe out and let the name stay there, warm. Sometimes just saying a name brings someone closer.
Sampati. The wingless old vulture who comes for a meal, hears his brother's name, and becomes family.

600.title: Sampati
600.hook: two young brothers race toward the sun
600.carry: the wings that saved his brother
600.howItsDone: Storytellers often pair Sampati's sacrifice for Jatayu with Jatayu's sacrifice for Sita: two brothers, each burned or wounded for someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati heard his brother Jatayu's name and turned from hunter to mourner. Who speaks of my brother?

Two brothers race straight up toward the sun. It's day six hundred, and Sampati is telling the monkeys how it began. When Jatayu and I were young, he says, we were proud of our flying. We were rivals the way brothers are, each sure he was the stronger. So one day we raced. It's an old kind of contest: two brothers, each needing to win, neither willing to turn back first.
screen: `A RACE TOWARD THE SUN.` → `DAY SIX HUNDRED.` → `TWO PROUD YOUNG BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: They climbed until the earth below looked small. Then the heat came. Jatayu, the younger, began to faint, and Sampati spread his own wings over his brother to shade him. His wings burned. He fell, landed here on the Vindhya hills, and has lived without wings ever since. So the wings he's missing are the wings that saved his brother. The race was for pride; the burn was for his brother. Then he waited, a long time. A sage named Nishakara lived on this mountain. He comforted Sampati and told him that one day Rama's messengers would come searching for Sita, and if Sampati helped them, his wings would grow back. Like Shabari, he was told to wait for Rama's people. Without wings he couldn't hunt, so his son Suparshva brought him food. One day Suparshva came back late and empty-handed. He had seen a dark giant flying over the sea carrying a weeping woman, and had stood aside to let them pass. That was Ravana, Sampati tells the monkeys. That was your Sita. And the monkeys, who sat down to die an hour ago, sit up straight.
screen: `SAMPATI SHADES HIS BROTHER.` · `THE WINGS BURN.` · `NISHAKARA'S PROMISE.` · `SUPARSHVA SAW RAVANA.`

segments.voice: Let your arms rest open a little, like folded wings, and think of someone you once protected, or who protected you. Breathe in the shelter that was given; breathe out and let any cost of it be there too. Love sometimes costs something, and you can sit with both.

601.title: Sampati
601.hook: a vulture's sight reaches Lanka, and his wings grow back
601.carry: this is the sign that you'll succeed
601.howItsDone: The Kishkindha Kanda closes on the shore with the question of who can cross the sea; in recitations, Sampati's vision is the turning point that sends listeners into the Sundara Kanda, which some families recite on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati, who burned his wings shading his brother, and whose son saw Ravana fly over the sea.

Where is she? That's the only question that matters now, and Sampati can answer it. Vultures, he tells the monkeys, see very far. We're born with it. Our food is far below us, so our eyes reach far. From this hill I can see a hundred yojanas, across the whole sea. The monkeys turn and look where he's looking. All they can see is water.
screen: `WHERE IS SHE?` → `A VULTURE'S SIGHT.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS.`

segments.voice: Sampati looks south and tells them what he sees. An island, a hundred yojanas away. On it, Lanka, a golden city built by Vishvakarma, the architect of the gods. And in it, kept in Ravana's inner grounds and guarded by rakshasa women, is Sita, dressed in yellow silk, grieving. The answer doesn't come from the armies, the kings or the planned search routes. It comes from an old, wingless bird who an hour ago wanted to eat them. Then the old promise comes true. Because Sampati has helped Rama's messengers, his wings begin to grow, right there in front of them. New feathers. He feels young and strong again, and he tells them: this is the sign that you'll succeed. Make the effort. Cross the sea. Then he spreads his new wings and flies off, to see whether he can still fly. A whole thread ties off today. Two brothers: one fell trying to stop Ravana in the sky, and the other saw where Ravana went. What one began, the other finished from a hilltop. Now the monkeys know where Sita is. Between them and her lies a hundred yojanas of open sea, and one question left: who can cross it?
screen: `LANKA, ACROSS THE SEA.` · `SITA IN RAVANA'S GROUNDS.` · `SAMPATI'S WINGS GROW BACK.` · `TWO BROTHERS, ONE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze go as far as it can, out a window, down a hallway, or to the farthest wall, and rest your eyes there. Breathe in and let your sight be wide; breathe out and soften it. A spy from Lanka came over and told the army where she was.
Sugriva's search plans pointed them straight to the right island.
chat.meaning: With a vulture's far sight, Sampati saw Sita in Lanka, a hundred yojanas over the sea, and his wings grew back.

602.title: the leap decided
602.hook: a hundred yojanas of water, and a circle of monkeys saying out loud how far each of them can jump
602.carry: no one could promise a hundred
602.howItsDone: Readers of the Kishkindha Kanda often linger on this scene of the monkeys stating their limits on the shore, because it sets up the moment when Jambavan turns to Hanuman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sampati's wings grew back as he told the monkeys where Sita was. Across the sea, in Lanka.

The job is finally clear, and it's impossible. Sita is in Lanka, an island a hundred yojanas across the ocean. A yojana is an old measure of distance, many miles long. The monkeys walk down to the shore and look at the water. Valmiki describes it like something alive: huge waves, sea creatures, a roar that never stops. The whole army sits down on the sand, quiet. Nobody wants to say the obvious thing first.
screen: `THE JOB IS CLEAR.` → `A HUNDRED YOJANAS OF SEA.` → `THE ARMY SITS DOWN, QUIET.`

segments.voice: Angada, the young prince who leads them, breaks the silence: who here can cross this? One by one, the monkeys answer honestly. One says he can leap ten yojanas. Another, twenty. Another, thirty. On it goes, each a little further, up to the old bear Jambavan, who says ninety. When he was young, he adds, he could have done it easily. He once circled the great god Vishnu when Vishnu strode across the worlds in three steps. But age has taken that. Then Angada speaks. He thinks he can jump the full hundred. What he isn't sure of is the jump back. Jambavan answers kindly but firmly. You're the leader, the root of the whole expedition. You don't send the root. Nobody brags here, and nobody pretends. Each monkey says what he can actually do, the numbers fall short, and that's allowed. It closes a week that ran from Svayamprabha's hidden cave, where precious time was lost underground, to Sampati, who lost his wings saving his brother and got them back helping strangers, to a beach of honest numbers that don't add up to a hundred. One monkey hasn't spoken. He's sitting apart, saying nothing at all.
screen: `WHO CAN CROSS THIS?` · `TEN, TWENTY, THIRTY... NINETY.` · `ANGADA: I'M NOT SURE OF THE WAY BACK.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T SEND THE ROOT.` · then: `ONE MONKEY HASN'T SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels too far to cross: a task, a conversation, a long recovery. Instead of measuring the whole distance, ask honestly how far you can go today, ten yojanas or twenty, and hold that number without shame. With each breath out, let the gap between what you can do and what is needed simply be true, for now.
Yojana, an old measure of distance many miles long: what the monkeys count in as each says how far he can jump, and the numbers fall short of a hundred.
Your line: no one could promise a hundred. Not yet, anyway. Day six hundred two, done.

original.note: Sanskrit yojana, an old unit of distance; its exact length varies by source.

trapdoor: what you thought: the monkeys were all heroes who could do anything.
what it means: on the shore, each one names an honest limit, and none of the numbers reaches a hundred.
what a scholar hears: Jambavan's memory of circling Vishnu's three strides points to the Vamana story of Vishnu's three strides across the worlds, a story told in other Hindu texts as well.
recall: a finger-ring with Rama's name on it

chat.says: Why didn't Angada just make the jump himself? He said he could.
options: Unsure of the jump back, and Jambavan said you don't send the leader.
He was too scared of the sea monsters Valmiki describes there.
He thought someone younger and faster should have the honor.
chat.meaning: Angada could leap a hundred but doubted the return; Jambavan called him the root of the expedition, and you don't send the root.
